meta.title: Who really said "To give real service you must add something which cannot be bought or measured with money, and that is sincerity and integrity"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Douglas Adams. Donald A. Adams, president of Rotary International, said it in a 1926 convention address printed in The Rotarian.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'To give real service you must add something which cannot be bought or measured with money, and that is sincerity and integrity'?
meta.ogDescription: Douglas Adams wasn't born until 1952. The line is Donald A. Adams's, from a 1926 Rotarian address — the Douglas credit first shows up in 2002.

answer.label: Not Douglas Adams — actually Donald A. Adams
answer.authorDates: President of Rotary International · spoke the line in a 1926 convention address
answer.sourceLine: The line comes from “Rotary’s Ideal of Service,” the convention address of Rotary International president Donald A. Adams, printed in The Rotarian in August 1926 — a different Adams entirely, and one who was speaking to a service club about business ethics. Douglas Adams was not born until 1952, and the earliest printing that credits him which Quote Investigator documents is a South Carolina newspaper page from 2002. One more wrinkle: Donald A. Adams’s own sentence ended “…and that thing is sincerity and integrity” — the smoother wording everyone quotes today was trimmed by a newspaper in 1932.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: “Rotary’s Ideal of Service: Convention Address of the President”
Donald A. Adams, President of Rotary International
Vol. 29, no. 2 — article begins p. 8; quotation on p. 60, col. 3

source.excerpt: We should all put into practice the Golden Rule of dealing with the other fellow as we would like to have him deal with us. But Service is something more than selling goods which are all wool and a yard wide and making delivery according to the contract. To give real service you must add something which cannot be bought or measured with money and that thing is sincerity and integrity.
trail: August 1926 — Quote Investigator ↗ traces the line to the convention address of Rotary International president Donald A. Adams, printed in The Rotarian. His sentence ends “…and that thing is sincerity and integrity.”

6 February 1932 — the Elmira Star-Gazette reprints it in a column called “Thoughts On Life” with “thing” removed and a comma added. That trimmed sentence is the one the internet still circulates, and it ran under Donald A. Adams’s name ↗. The credit then holds through a 1937 Forbes anthology and collections as late as 1995.

1947, then 2002 — a Georgia newspaper column prints it as “D. A. Adams,” and QI points to exactly that kind of initials-only credit as the likely cause of the drift. The first printing crediting Douglas Adams that QI documents ↗ is The Times and Democrat of Orangeburg, South Carolina, on 21 March 2002.

The timing settles it — Douglas Adams was born on 11 March 1952 and died on 11 May 2001 ↗. The line had been in print under another man’s name for a quarter of a century before he was born, and the credit only moved to him after his death.
source.excerptNote: Transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗ from the Google Books full view of the issue. Note the difference from the popular version: Adams said “and that thing is sincerity and integrity.” The word was dropped and a comma added when the Elmira Star-Gazette reprinted the line on 6 February 1932 — still crediting Donald A. Adams.

source.rightsNote: The sentence was first published in The Rotarian in August 1926, well before the 1931 cutoff, so the text is in the public domain in the United States. The shortened wording that circulates today is a one-word deletion made by a newspaper in 1932 — a trivial alteration to an already public-domain sentence, not new authorship, so it carries no separate claim.

author.name: Donald A. Adams
author.kicker: The man who actually said it
author.heading: Donald A. Adams
author.metaLine: President of Rotary International · author of the 1926 convention address “Rotary’s Ideal of Service”
author.bio: Donald A. Adams was president of Rotary International when he delivered the convention address published as “Rotary’s Ideal of Service” in the August 1926 issue of The Rotarian, the organisation’s official magazine. The passage about sincerity and integrity sits inside a plain-spoken argument that service means more than shipping honest goods on time. He was credited by name in print for close to seventy years — in a 1932 newspaper column, in B. C. Forbes’s Thoughts on the Business of Life in 1937, and in quotation collections as late as 1995 — before the line quietly changed hands.

misattribution.heading: How the wrong Adams got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is a surname collision that a set of initials turned into a permanent swap. Two men named Adams, seventy-odd years apart, and only one of them ever said it.

items.why: Quote databases print it under his name with no source attached — Goodreads ↗ and AZQuotes ↗ both credit Douglas Adams and cite nothing, and it has spread from there into business and ministry material such as Busted Halo ↗. He was born on 11 March 1952 ↗, long after the line was in print.

A 1947 Georgia newspaper column printed the quotation credited only to “D. A. Adams.” Quote Investigator ↗ notes that this use of initials can cause confusion, and suggests an ambiguous “D. Adams” is what let the credit slide from the obscure Donald to the famous Douglas.

Even the popular string is not quite what was said. Adams’s 1926 text ends “…and that thing is sincerity and integrity”; the word was dropped and a comma added when the Elmira Star-Gazette reprinted it on 6 February 1932, still under his name ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Donald A. Adams, president of Rotary International, said it in the convention address published in The Rotarian in August 1926 — and Quote Investigator ↗ dates the first printing that credits Douglas Adams to a Chamber of Commerce page in The Times and Democrat of Orangeburg, South Carolina, on 21 March 2002.

context.heading: A service-club speech, not a science-fiction novel
lead: Read the sentence next to the paragraph it came from and the Douglas Adams attribution falls apart on tone alone. The 1926 original is a Rotary president telling a room of businessmen that shipping goods “all wool and a yard wide” and delivering on contract is not yet service — you have to add something you cannot invoice for. It is earnest civic-club rhetoric, and it is the opposite of the register Douglas Adams wrote in.

What makes this case unusually tidy is that the paper trail never really went cold. Donald A. Adams kept his credit through a 1932 newspaper column, a 1937 Forbes anthology and quotation collections into the 1990s. The swap looks less like a myth than like a filing error that stuck.
detailsBody: Donald A. Adams said: “…something which cannot be bought or measured with money and that thing is sincerity and integrity.” The version in every quote database drops “thing” and adds a comma, which is smoother and slightly more quotable.

Quote Investigator dates that alteration to the Elmira Star-Gazette of 6 February 1932, where it still ran under Donald A. Adams’s name. So the famous string is a newspaper’s tidy-up of a 1926 sentence — genuinely his thought and very nearly his words, but not his exact ones.
context.pull: A 1947 column printed it as “D. A. Adams.” Two initials were all it took.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator concludes Donald A. Adams originated the statement in a speech published in The Rotarian in August 1926; the 1926 text reads 'and that thing is sincerity and integrity'; the word 'thing' was removed and a comma added in the Elmira Star-Gazette of 6 February 1932, still credited to Donald A. Adams; a 1947 West Point (Georgia) column credited 'D. A. Adams'; and The Times and Democrat of 21 March 2002 is the first printing QI documents crediting Douglas Adams. QI also notes Douglas Adams was born in 1952.

This Google Books volume is The Rotarian, August 1926, published by Rotary International (the issue QI cites for the original address). Volume metadata confirmed by fetch; the page-60 text itself is not extractable from the page, so the wording is cited as QI's transcription rather than as an independent reading of the scan.
Douglas Adams was born 11 March 1952 and died 11 May 2001; he was an English author, screenwriter and humorist best known for The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy.
The Rotarian is Rotary International's official monthly magazine, first published in 1911 (as The National Rotarian).

Goodreads attributes 'To give real service you must add something which cannot be bought or measured with money, and that is sincerity and integrity' to Douglas Adams, with no source book or publication listed.
AZQuotes attributes the quotation to Douglas Adams, printing the popular wording exactly as it circulates.
Busted Halo publishes the quotation as a ministry resource credited to Douglas Adams, showing the misattribution's spread beyond quote databases.
Quote Investigator maintains a Douglas Adams tag archive indexing the quotations credited to him that it has investigated, including several it reassigns to other originators.
